Introduction to Respiratory System Procedures

Welcome to Respiratory System Procedures.

This unit covers the following sections:

  • Anatomy and Physiology of the Respiratory System
  • Radiopharmaceuticals for Lung Imaging
  • Clinical Applications (Indications, PE, COPD, Lung Quantification)
  • Imaging Procedures (Ventilation and Perfusion)
  • Case Studies

There is a cumulative homework/quiz to complete when you finish all sections.

2

Respiratory System A&P Overview

Respiratory System A & P:

In this first section you will find:

  • Anatomy and Physiology of the Respiratory System
    • 1. Introduction
    • 2. Organs of the Respiratory System
      • a. Nose
      • b. Pharynx
      • c. Larynx
      • d. Trachea
    • 3. Bronchi
    • 4. Lungs
      • a. Anatomy
      • b. Breathing
    • 5. Pathology

  • As you can see, the respiratory system is a complex unit with many organs in it.
  • All of the organs serve a vital purpose to the human body.
  • We will break each organ down and discuss it.
  • The Respiratory system is only good for breathing Right? Wrong!
  • The Respiratory system Supplies Oxygen to the body & eliminates wastes
  • Failure of this system results in death of cells – that's BAD

Before we see how this works, lets look at what makes it happen!

3

Organs of the Respiratory System

Organs of the Respiratory System

  • As you saw from the picture, there is more to the respiratory system than just the Lungs
    • Upper Respiratory System
      • Nose & Pharynx
    • Lower Respiratory System
      • Larynx, Trachea, Bronchi, & Lungs

The Nose

  • As you just saw, the nose comes in all different sizes and shapes
  • The Framework of the nose is made up of
    • 1. Bone
    • 2. Cartilage
  • The nose is covered by muscle and skin
    • Since it has a muscle, could I work out my nose at the gym?

Function of the Nose

  • The nose doesn't just take in air for breathing
  • The nose will also:
    • 1. Warm, moisten, & filter incoming air
    • 2. Olfactory (smelling) stimuli are received
    • 3. Modify speech sounds

The Pharynx

  • The pharynx is basically a fancy term for the throat
    • Pharynx is Greek for "throat"
  • The pharynx starts at the back of the nose and ends up at the top of the Larynx
  • The pharynx is made up of muscles and lined with mucous membranes
  • The Pharynx is a passageway for air and food and provides a resonating chamber for speech sounds

The Larynx

  • Larynx (voice box) lies in the lower section of the Pharynx
  • The Larynx connects the Pharynx to the Trachea
  • The larynx is composed of cartilage
  • The larynx is involved in more than just speech
    • The Larynx contains thyroid cartilage, epiglottis, & arytenoid cartilage
    • Let's briefly discuss each of these
  • The Larynx is also involved in:
    • 1. Regulation of airflow during breathing
    • 2. Protection of the airway

Thyroid Cartilage

  • Thyroid Cartilage – Adams apple
  • THIS HAS NOTHING TO DO WITH THE THYROID GLAND
  • 2 fused plates of cartilage that lie ANT to the vocal cords
  • Serve as protection for the vocal cords
  • Do women have an Adam's apple?
    • Yes; it's just smaller than a man's so it's not really noticeable

Epiglottis

  • Large leaf-shaped piece of cartilage
  • Acts like a trap door
  • When you swallow, the epiglottis covers the opening to the trachea
  • All food & liquids are routed to the esophagus to go to the stomach rather than the trachea which leads to the lungs

Arytenoid Cartilage

  • Cartilage that is attached to the vocal cords & muscles of the pharynx
  • These muscles can move the cartilage that will move the vocal cords

Trachea

  • Trachea (AKA windpipe)
  • Located ANT to the esophagus
  • Extends from the Larynx to the Bronchi
  • The trachea is a fixed open tube used for the transportation of air to the lungs
  • The INF portion of the Trachea divides into the right & left BRONCHI

Since we mentioned bronchi, Let's go there................

4

Bronchi

Bronchi

  • The trachea divides into the Bronchi
    • Right Primary Bronchus & Left Primary Bronchus
  • Each of which goes into their respective lung
  • Right is more vertical, shorter, and wider
  • An object is more likely to get lodged in the Right lung
  • On entering the lungs, the Primary Bronchi divide to form smaller Bronchi
  • Secondary Bronchi
    • You have one secondary bronchi for each lobe of each lung
    • Right lung has 3 lobes and 3 secondary bronchi
    • Left lung has 2 lobes and 2 secondary bronchi
  • The secondary branch to form smaller bronchi called Tertiary Bronchi
  • And finally the Tertiary Bronchi form the Terminal Bronchioles

Bronchial Terms

  • Bronchial Tree – As the Bronchi taper down, it appears as the branches of a tree
    • The branching is referred to as the Bronchi tree
  • Bronchography - examining the bronchial tree
  • Bronchoscope - visual exam of the bronchi tree uses a bronchoscope
5

Lungs

Lungs

  • 2 paired cone-shaped organs
  • The lungs lie in the thoracic cavity
  • The lungs rest on the diaphragm and extend to the clavicles
  • Each lie against the ribs ANT & POST

Anatomy of the Lungs

  • Base – the broad INF portion of the lungs
    • Concave shape so it can fit over the diaphragm
  • Apex – the narrow SUP portion of the lungs
  • Hilus – the region of the lungs where the bronchi, blood vessels, lymphatic vessels and nerves enter & exit
  • The lungs are 2 paired organs, but they are not exactly the same

Characteristics of each Lung

  • The Right lung is thicker, broader & shorter
    • B/c the diaphragm is higher on the right side due to the diaphragm resting on the liver
  • Right has 3 lobes and the Left has 2
    • each lobe has it's own secondary bronchus
  • Cardiac Notch – the left lung contains a concave notch where the heart lies
    • The cardiac notch shows up as an attenuated area on a CXR & lung scan

Pleural Membrane

  • Collectively it is 2 layers of membranes
    • Don't worry about what they are, just what they do
  • They protect and enclose each lung
  • Between these membranes is the pleural cavity
    • The pleural cavity contains lubricating fluid
    • The fluid will reduce friction and allow the lungs to move easier during breathing

Alveoli

  • The alveoli are Sacs at the end of terminal bronchiole
  • The lungs have 250 - 300 million of them
  • They are lined w/ alveolar cells
  • Pulmonary capillaries lie in contact w/ the alveolar cells
  • Exchange of respiratory gases b/w the lungs and blood takes place by diffusion across alveolar cells and capillary walls
6

Breathing & Respiration

The lungs are used for Breathing

  • Breathing is a good thing!
  • The process of breathing is called respiration
  • Before we continue do as Mr. Meagi from karate kid said and, "Breathe in through nose, Out through mouth."
    • That's better – now that you got some Oxygen to your brains we can see why you just took that breath!
  • Why we Breathe
    • There are 2 main reasons why we need to breathe
      • 1. To get air in to tissues of the body
      • 2. To get rid of CO2 from those tissues
    • Why do we breathe automatically
      • Your bodies breathe to get rid of CO2
      • If your body suddenly did not have any CO2, you would stop breathing
  • How this process happens
    • Before inspiration air pressure in the lungs = atmospheric pressure (760 mmHg)
    • To get rid of the CO2 waste:
      • Air is inhaled & passes through pharynx, larynx, & trachea and enters the lungs
      • During inspiration the diaphragm contracts and sucks in air b/c the pressure drops
    • When the diaphragm contracts it actually flattens b/c normally it is concave shaped
    • For expiration to occur the diaphragm relaxes & the pressure inside the lungs goes back to atmospheric pressure and air is forced out
    • We breathe 30,000 times/day
      • Your next assignment is to count how many times you breath in a day
7

Lung Pathology

Lung Pathology

  • 1. Hemothorax - pleural cavity fills w/ blood
  • 2. Pneumothorax - pleural cavity fills w/ air
    • Usually from a surgical opening, stab or gunshot
    • Can cause lung to collapse (atelectasis)
  • 3. Pleurisy - inflammation of the pleural membrane
    • Causes back & chest pain from friction between the parietal and visceral layers
  • 4. Repiratory Failure
    • Respiratory system can not supply sufficient O2 or can not eliminate enough CO2 to prevent acidosis
  • 4. Hypos
    • Low level of O2 in the body
  • 5. Carbon Monoxide (CO) Poisoning
    • CO comes from exhaust fumes, tobacco smoke and wood or coal burning stoves
    • CO binds with the heme of a RBC and decreasing the amount of O2 that binds with a RBC
    • This can lead to hypox

Now we can look at some of the bigger diseases..........

  • 6. Pneumonia
    • Acute infection or inflammation of the alveoli
    • Sacs filled w/ fluid and dead WBC
    • Air space for gas exchange is reduced
    • Usually caused by a bacterial or fungi
    • Elderly, infants, immunocompromised pt's, smokers are susceptible to pheumonia
  • 7. Tuberculosis
    • Bacteria that usually infects the lungs
    • Destroys parts of the lung tissue & it's replaced by connective tissue
      • makes the lungs less elastic
    • Spread by inhalation and exhalation
    • Can w/stand many disinfectants but die in sunlight – go figure
    • TB is treatable!
  • 8. Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease - (COPD)
    • COPD is the obstruction or narrowing of the air passages of the lungs.
    • 16 million people have COPD and 100,000 die from it each year
    • Causes of COPD
      • 80% is from smoking
      • 20% from air pollutants
    • Types of COPD
      • Asthma, Bronchitis, & Emphysema
    • Signs and Symptoms of COPD
      • Cough - possibly w/ phlegm
      • Breathlessness - especially on exertion
      • Wheezing
      • Dyspnea – painful or labored breathing
  • Different types of COPD
  • Asthma - inflammatory disorder producing difficulty in breathing
    • Causes wheezing and a tight chest
    • Most common form is from an allergic rxn
      • pollen, mold, dust, animal hair
    • Can also be caused from:
      • infection, exposure to cold, exercise, fatigue, fumes, emotionally & psychological factors
    • Not caused by smoking
  • Emphysema is a destruction of lung tissue
    • Usually in the alveolar walls
    • Produces air spaces in lungs
    • The decreased air space causes less space for gas
  • Bronchitis- Inflammation of the bronchi
    • Causes the lungs to have excessive mucus
    • Causes recurrent lung infections
    • Causes a chronic cough
  • Treatments for COPD
    • Usually a form of a steroid med
      • cortisone
    • Bronchodialators – used to open airways
      • Theophylline (Theo-Dur or Elixophyllin)
    • Stop smoking is the best treatment

9. Pulmonary Embolism (PE)

  • Clot in a pulmonary vessel that obstructs circulation to lung tissue
  • Could be a blood clot or other foreign sub
  • Most PE originate from DVT
    • Usually from surgery, pt's w/ cancer, pregnancy, older people, badly broken bones
  • Women are at a higher risk
  • Smoking and birth control pills can also cause a PE
  • S & S of a PE:
    • Signs and symptoms of pulmonary embolism may be similar to those of a heart attack. They include:
    • Sudden chest pain •chronic cough - sometimes mixed with blood-streaked sputum •severe dyspnea (difficulty in breathing) •excessive perspiring •shock •cyanosis (bluish skin color) •anxiety •loss of consciousness
  • Treatment of a PE:
    • The line of defense for a PE is:
      • 1. Use meds to prevent more clots - Heparin, anticoagulants
      • 2. Use meds to dissolve clots - Steptokinase
      • 3. Surgically remove a clot
      • 4. A filter can be placed in a vein to prevent a clot from reaching the lung

To start talking about the Lung Scan let's look at the Radiopharmaceuticals.....

8

Intro to Respiratory Radiopharmaceuticals

Intro to Respiratory RP's:

  • Nuclear Medicine is very effective in diagnosing Respiratory Disorders
  • We will take a look at how radiopharmacueticals can localize in the lungs to allow us to diagnose diseases
  • We will start out by looking at each radiopharmaceutical

Radiopharmaceuticals for the Respiratory System can be broken down into 2 categories:

  • 1. Localize by following the air flow (Ventilation)
  • 2. Localize by following the blood stream (Perfusion)
9

Ventilation Agents

Ventilation Agents

Ventilation agents can also be broken down into 2 forms:

  • 1. Radioactive Inert Gases
    • 133Xe
    • 127Xe & 81mKr
  • 2. Radiolabeled Aerosols
    • 99mTc-DTPA

Inert Gases

  • Just as it says, ventilation agents are looking at the air flow of the lungs
  • Radioactive Inert Gases are already in the form of what we breath (gases)
  • This makes for a quick and easy determination of air flow
  • Past Inert Gas RP's
  • 1. 127Xe
    • Expensive and not as readily available
  • 2. 81mKr
    • Has a T1/2 of 13 seconds, therefore generators have to be on-site
    • Expensive and Inconvenient
  • The inert gas most commonly used is 133Xe....

Xenon-133 used for Ventilation

  • When 133Xe is inhaled it follows the bronchial tree and localizes.
  • If an area is blocked and not getting air, 133Xe will not go there.
    • Shows a cold spot

Advantages and Disadvantages of Xe-133

  • Advantages
    • 1. 133Xe is pretty cheap!
      • Remember it's a byproduct of fission
    • 2. 133Xe is more sensitive for COPD than radiolabeled aerosols
    • 3. 133Xe is quicker for scanning(1/2 of the time of radiolabeled aerosols)
    • 4. Perfusion uses 99mTc, therefore the different energy of 133Xe is beneficial
    • 5. Rapid clearance of 133Xe from the lungs (biologic T1/2 of 30 sec)
  • Disadvantages
    • 1. Low Energy causes 1/2 of it's photons to by attenuated
    • 2. Need a special room design
      • Negative air pressure to outside hallway
      • Xenon trap in the room to collect the Xenon gas
    • 3. Patient cooperation
      • Pt must breathe on a closed spirometer for several minute
    • 4. Do Not get multiple Views for ventilation (only POST)

Radiolabeled Aerosols

  • Radiolabeled Aerosols end result is the same as using Inert Gas
  • 99mTc-DTPA is used as a radiolabeled aerosol
  • Radiolabeled Aerosols use an Ultrasonic Nebulizer to form the aerosol
  • The effects and use of radiolabeled aerosols are totally different than using Inert Gases

Advantages and Disadvantages of 99mTc-DTPA

  • Advantages
    • 1. We are using 99mTc
      • Readily available and has good imaging characteristics
    • 2. 99mTc-DTPA stays in the lungs longer
      • Permits multiple views
    • 2. Not as much Patient cooperation is necessary
    • 3. No special room design
      • The inhalation doesn't have to be in the camera room
  • Disadvantages
    • 1. Only 2 - 10% of the dose is actually delivered to the patient
      • Only 1 - 2 mCi gets to the patient's lungs
    • 2. Both Ventilation and perfusion uses 99mTc
    • 3. Don't get Single breath or washout views
10

Perfusion Agents

Perfusion Agents

  • Perfusion imaging requires a particle labeled to a radionuclide
  • 99mTc-MAA (Macroaggregated Albumin) is the most common RP
    • 99mTc-Pulmolite is very similar to 99mTc-MAA and can also be used
    • 1 - 5 mCi will be injected
  • 99mTc-MAA will localize in the lungs by capillary blockage
    • 95% of particles will localize in lungs on 1st pass
    • Want a minimum of 100,000 particles but usually 200,000 - 700,000
    • Size should be 5 - 100 um (most are 10- 30 μm)
  • A PE will inhibit the particles from localizing in a segment of the lungs
  • Other than a PE these Particles will generally block 1 in 1000 normal capillaries
    • All other capillaries are free and open for oxygen

Let's look at how we image with these RP's

11

Respiratory Imaging Overview

Respiratory Imaging

Ventilation Imaging

  • The ultimate goal of ventilation imaging is the same no matter what radiopharmaceutical we use
  • Ventilation imaging determines
    • 1. COPD defects (regional ventilation)
    • 2. Distinguishes b/w COPD and PE
  • Depending on which RP we use, the procedure is totally different
  • The Ventilation scan is generally performed first
12

¹³³Xe Ventilation Imaging

133Xe Imaging

  • 10 - 20 mCi of 133Xe will be placed on a gas generator
  • The gas is pumped in to the generator
  • The patient is placed supine or upright with the camera POST
    • POST gives the best view using 133Xe
    • POST has the least amount of attenuation
    • POST is the only view taken using 133Xe
  • The patient is hooked up to a facemask or mouthpiece

133Xe uses 3 phases for imaging:

  • 1. Single wash-in or initial breath
    • Pt will exhale as much as possible
    • Pt will then inhale 133Xe and hold their breath for 15 sec
    • A static image is taken
    • Represents regional ventilation
    • Detects 66% of ventilation defects
  • 2. Equilibrium
    • Pt rebreaths the expired 133Xe with 2 L of oxygen for 2 - 5 min
    • The rebreathing is contained in a closed system
    • A static image is taken
    • Least sensitive for defects but is essential for a good washout
    • Represents the distribution of lung volume
  • 3. Washout Phase
    • 133Xe is stopped
    • Patient breaths fresh air or oxygen for 2 - 3 minutes
    • 15 sec serial images are taken
    • 133Xe should clear w/i 2 - 3 min
    • Retention of 133Xe results in air trapping or obstructive diseases
    • Detects 90% of obstructive airway diseases
  • That concludes imaging with 133Xe
    • The 3 phases take approximately 15 minutes to complete
    • The Patient can immediately move on the perfusion scan
      • The pt stays on the imaging table for the perfusion scan
13

⁹⁹ᵐTc-DTPA Aerosol Imaging

Tc-99m Aerosol Imaging

  • The procedure for aerosol imaging is totally different
    • 1. 30 mCi of 99mTc-DTPA is loaded into a Nebulizer in a volume of 2 - 3 ml
    • 2. Connect Oxygen to the nebulizer
      • Oxygen runs over the 99mTc-DTPA and picks it up to give us a radiolabeled aerosol
    • 3. Administer the aerosol to the patient with a mouthpiece
      • Pt should be supine to allow for an even distribution
      • Flow the Oxygen at a rate of 10 L/min
    • 4. The patient should breath for 5 - 10 min
      • Allows for .5 - 1.0 mCi of activity to localize in the lungs
      • 150K cpm should localize in the lungs
      • Allows for decent imaging times
      • Longer inhalation doesn't hurt but isn't necessary and is harder on the patient
    • 5. Images are taken with the patient upright or supine
    • 6. Six images are taken for 200K - 300K counts
      • ANT, POST, R & L LAT, & POST OBLIQUES

The patient is now finished and can go into the perfusion!!

14

Perfusion Imaging

Perfusion Imaging

  • 1. 1 - 5 mCi of 99mTc-MAA are inj IV with the Pt supine
    • Inject slow (over 30 seconds)
    • DO NOT flush the syringe with blood
    • Both factors can cause clumps of particles in the lungs
  • 2. Take 6 images for 500K counts (remain consistent on your counts)
    • ANT, POST, R & L LAT, & POST OBLIQUES
    • POST is still the most important view to take
    • Put pt's arms above their head for the LAT views
      • limits attenuation

That's the whole Perfusion Procedure. Not Bad huh!! We've still got alot more fun to deal with though!!

Let's look at some images and diseases that go along with Lung Scans!!!

15

Indications for Lung Scan

Indication for a Lung Scan

There are several indications for a Lung scan.

  • Determine the likelihood of pulmonary embolism.
    • MOST of your lung scans are for a PE
    • This is the major study we will look at
  • Document the degree of resolution of pulmonary embolism.
  • Quantify differential pulmonary function before surgery.
  • Evaluate lung transplants.
  • Evaluate congenital heart or lung disease, such as shunts, pulmonary arterial stenosis, and arteriovenous fistulae and their treatment.
  • Confirm presence of bronchopleural fistula.
  • Evaluate chronic pulmonary parenchymal disorders such as cystic fibrosis.
  • Evaluate cause of pulmonary hypertension.
16

Segments of the Lung

Segments of the Lung

It's important to know the major Lobes of the Lung below:

  • Right Upper Lobe
  • Right Medial Lobe
  • Right Lower Lobe
  • Left Upper Lobe
  • Left Lower Lobe

You only need to know the lobe and not each individual segment

17

Pulmonary Embolism (PE)

Pulmonary Embolism

Most V/Q scans are completed to determine if a patient has a PE

What do we know about a PE?

  • When a patient comes in with Shortness of Breath and Chest Pain
    • We need to determine if those Symptoms are from a PE or possible an MI
  • It is a Mis-matched defect
    • Normal Ventilation
    • Abnormal defect on Perfusion
      • Defects are commonly wedge-shaped
  • A PE can occur in any area of the lungs but is most common in the lower lobes
    • Usually come from deep veins in the legs
  • There are 3 main types of PEs
    • Distal PE: A smaller clot that travels far into the lung periphery and blocks smaller vessels. This can cause pleuritic chest pain due to inflammation near the lung's outer lining.
    • Lobar PE: Occurs when a clot lodges in one of the larger, lobar branches of the pulmonary artery, blocking blood flow to a specific lobe of the lung.
    • Saddle PE: A rare but life-threatening type of PE caused by a large clot that straddles the bifurcation of the main pulmonary artery, obstructing blood flow to both lungs
  • How do we evaluate a PE
    • Compare the same view of the Ventilation and Perfusion
      • The Vent will be normal and the Perf will have 1 or multiple defects
        • Notice the multiple defects (arrows) in the Perfusion scans
18

COPD on Lung Scan

Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease

We don't normally do a Lung scan for COPD

  • A Pt knows they have COPD
  • We want to rule out that they have a PE

What does COPD look like on a Lung Scan

  • Ventilation
    • Patchy, non-uniform distribution
    • Tracer trapping (especially with Xenon washout)
    • Delayed/absent clearance on washout phase
  • Perfusion
    • Matched defect compared to Vent
    • Defects are NOT wedge shaped

How do we evaluate COPD

  • Look for a matched non-wedge shaped defect in both the VENT and PERF
19

Lung Quantification Study

Lung Quantification Study

Why are we performing a Lung Quantification Study

  • Measure the relative contribution of each lung or lung segment to overall function
  • Pre-surgical planning
    • Predict lung function after a lobectomy or pneumonectomy for lung cancer
    • It's kind of a risk vs benfit
  • Assessment of regional lung function
    • Determines how much each lung contributes to total ventilation and perfusion
    • Helps in conditions like COPD, bronchiectasis, pulmonary fibrosis, or after previous lung surgeries
  • Evaluation of perfusion/ventilation asymmetry
    • Detects whether one lung (or lobe) is underperforming due to obstruction, embolism, or chronic disease

How are we performing a Lung Quantification Study

  • Complete both a Ventilation and Perfusion scan
  • Draw a Region of Interest around each lung
  • Perform Data Analysis to determine the activity for each lung/segment

What are the normal percentages for Lung Quantification

  • Normal Right vs Left Lung Contributions
    • Right lung: ~55% of total function
    • Left lung: ~45% of total function
      • �� This slight asymmetry exists because the right lung has 3 lobes and is larger, while the left lung has 2 lobes and accommodates the heart.
    • Normal Lobar Contributions (approximate)
      • Right Lung (≈55%)
        • Upper lobe: 20%
        • Middle lobe: ~12%
        • Lower lobe: ~23%
      • Left Lung (≈45%)
        • Upper lobe (includes lingula): ~20%
        • Lower lobe: ~25%

What do we see on a Lung Quantification Study

    • Look at the ROI for each lung
    • ANT: Left - 44.9% | Right - 55.1%
    • POST: Left - 49.5% | Right - 50.5%
      • These are normal results
    • The Upper, Middle, and Lower Lobes and also be analyzed
20

Case Study 1

Lung Scan Case Studies

Lung Scan #1

  • This is 60 YO male with a Hx of CA
  • He had a sudden onset of SOB
  • We are evaluating for a possible PE

Lung Scan #1

Lung Scan #1 Results Perfusion Image

Lung Scan #1 Results Ventilation Image

📋 Scan Analysis:
  • Ventilation: Fairly uniform uptake; some focal uptake (possibly airway disease); activity in stomach (swallowed tracer)
  • Perfusion: Several defects in both lungs — R upper lung, Lat segment of R medial lung, L Superior lung, basal segment of L lung
  • All defects seen in multiple views and mismatched to Ventilation

→ HIGH PROBABILITY OF PE

21

Case Study 2

Lung Scan # 2

  • This Patient is a 22 YO male who had a sarcoma in his R leg
    • He had surgery on his leg
  • He has had SOB and Chest Pain after the surgery
  • Due to his symptoms the the prior surgery a lung scan was ordered to evaluate for a PE

Lung Scan #2

Lung Scan #2 Results Perfusion Image

📋 Scan Analysis:
  • Dramatic decrease in perfusion of the R lung — mismatched to Ventilation
  • Indicates a Massive PE in the R Lung (probably in primary or secondary bronchi)
  • Small defects in the L Base — matched to Ventilation (indicates Obstructive Airway Disease)

→ MASSIVE PE IN RIGHT LUNG

22

Case Study 3

Lung Scan # 3

  • This is a 28 YO male with sudden onset of Chest Pain
  • Pt has a Hx of R calf DVT
  • Lung scan is done to localize the pain
    • Is the pain coming from his heart or lungs
    • Evaluate PE

Lung Scan #3

Lung Scan #3 Results Perfusion Image

Lung Scan #3 Results Ventilation Image

📋 Scan Analysis:
  • Large perfusion defect at R Lung Base — mismatched defect, involving multiple segments of the R Lower Lobe
  • R Apex: questionable defect — mismatched, uncertain if artifact (attenuation) or PE

→ INTERMEDIATE PROBABILITY OF PE

23

Case Study 4

Lung Scan # 4

  • This is a 27 YO female with sickle cell anemia
  • She is having tachypnea, Tachycardia, & decreased arterial saturation (decreased Oxygen in the blood)
  • Evaluate for PE!

Lung Scan #4

Lung Scan #4 Results Perfusion Image

Lung Scan #4 Results Ventilation Image

📋 Scan Analysis:
  • 2 defects in the Post-Base of the L lung on Perfusion
  • Defects appear matched to the Ventilation scan
  • Matched defects suggest COPD rather than PE
  • Note: whenever a lung scan is positive (regardless of diagnosis) the report is usually "Low Probability of PE"

→ LOW PROBABILITY OF PE (possible COPD in L Post-Base)

24

Lung Scan # 5

  • He was sent to the ER due to chest pains and SOB
  • Evaluate for PE
  • The scan shows the Perfusion first and the Single Breath underneath
  • Only the POST image is shown b/c that is all that the pt could handle

Lung Scan #5

Lung Scan #5 Results Image

📋 Scan Analysis:

  • Large matched defect in the POST lobe of the left lung

Case Study 6

Lung Scan # 6

  • This lung scan was done on an 80 year old male with chest pain
  • Evaluate for PE
  • The images shows the RPO view for both the "Q" & "V" scans

Lung Scan #6

Lung Scan #6 Results Image

OK; Great job on the Respiratory System!!

📋 Scan Analysis:

Glossary

Ventilation (V)
The movement of air into and out of the lungs.
Perfusion (Q)
The flow of blood through the pulmonary capillaries.
V/Q Scan
Combined ventilation/perfusion lung scan used to evaluate for pulmonary embolism.
Pulmonary Embolism (PE)
A blood clot that travels to the pulmonary arteries, blocking blood flow. Shows as a mismatched defect (normal vent, abnormal perf).
COPD
Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease. Shows as matched defects on V/Q scan with tracer trapping on washout.
Mismatched Defect
Normal ventilation with abnormal perfusion defect — classic sign of PE.
Matched Defect
Defect present on both ventilation and perfusion — indicates COPD or obstructive airway disease.
¹³³Xe
Xenon-133; a radioactive inert gas used for ventilation imaging. Three phases: wash-in, equilibrium, washout.
⁹⁹ᵐTc-DTPA
Technetium-99m DTPA aerosol used for ventilation imaging. Loaded into a nebulizer and inhaled.
⁹⁹ᵐTc-MAA
Technetium-99m Macroaggregated Albumin; used for perfusion imaging via capillary blockade.
Capillary Blockade
Mechanism of ⁹⁹ᵐTc-MAA localization: particles (5–100 µm) lodge in pulmonary capillaries on first pass.
Atelectasis
Collapse of part or all of a lung, can result from pneumothorax.
Pneumothorax
Air in the pleural cavity; can cause lung collapse.
Hemothorax
Blood in the pleural cavity.
Pleurisy
Inflammation of the pleural membrane causing chest/back pain.
Nebulizer
Device used to convert liquid ⁹⁹ᵐTc-DTPA to a radiolabeled aerosol for inhalation.
Wash-in Phase
First phase of ¹³³Xe imaging: patient inhales and holds breath for 15 sec. Static image taken.
Equilibrium Phase
Second phase of ¹³³Xe imaging: patient rebreathes ¹³³Xe with O₂ for 2–5 min.
Washout Phase
Third phase of ¹³³Xe imaging: patient breathes room air; delayed clearance indicates airway disease.
Lung Quantification
Study measuring relative contribution of each lung/lobe to total function; used for pre-surgical planning.
Lobectomy
Surgical removal of a lobe of the lung.
Pneumonectomy
Surgical removal of an entire lung.
Saddle PE
Life-threatening PE where clot straddles the bifurcation of the main pulmonary artery.
Lobar PE
PE where clot lodges in a lobar branch, blocking blood flow to one lobe.
Distal PE
Smaller clot that travels far into lung periphery; may cause pleuritic chest pain.
Right Lung
Has 3 lobes (upper, middle, lower); contributes ~55% of total pulmonary function.
Left Lung
Has 2 lobes (upper, lower); accommodates the heart; contributes ~45% of total pulmonary function.
MAA Particle Count
Minimum 100,000 particles required; typically 200,000–700,000 injected for perfusion imaging.
MAA Particle Size
5–100 µm; most particles 10–30 µm. Blocks 1 in 1,000 normal capillaries.
Posterior (POST) View
Most important view for lung scanning; least attenuation. Only view taken with ¹³³Xe.
